articles.title: Trump to award Congressional Space Medal of Honor to Artemis II astronauts
articles.summary: The Artemis II crew will receive the Congressional Space Medal of Honor after becoming the first humans in more than 50 years to travel beyond the Moon. Their 10-day Orion mission also carried them farther into space than anyone in history.
articles.content:
President Donald J. Trump will present the Congressional Space Medal of Honor to each member of NASA's Artemis II crew during a ceremony at Johnson Space Center in Houston. The event is scheduled for 11 a.m. EDT on Friday, Aug. 28.

The medal is one of the highest honors associated with human spaceflight in the United States. It recognizes astronauts whose achievements have made an exceptional contribution to the nation's space program.

Artemis II Made Human Spaceflight History

NASA astronauts Reid Wiseman, Victor Glover, and Christina Koch, along with CSA (Canadian Space Agency) astronaut Jeremy Hansen, completed a 10-day mission around the Moon on April 10.

The flight marked the first time astronauts had traveled aboard NASA's Orion spacecraft, which is designed to carry crews on missions beyond low Earth orbit. Artemis II served as a major test of the spacecraft and its systems with humans on board.

During the mission, the crew became the first people in more than 50 years to travel beyond the Moon. They also ventured farther into space than any humans had ever traveled before, setting a new distance record for human spaceflight.

A Major Honor for the Artemis II Crew

The Aug. 28 ceremony will recognize the crew's role in advancing NASA's Artemis program and returning astronauts to deep space.

NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman will join President Trump and the four astronauts for the awards ceremony at Johnson Space Center.

**What happened** – On August 28, President Donald J. Trump awarded the Congressional Space Medal of Honor to the four Artemis II astronauts: Reid Wiseman, Victor Glover, Christina Koch, and Jeremy Hansen from the Canadian Space Agency. The ceremony took place at NASA's Johnson Space Center in Houston.

**Impact** – This medal is one of the highest awards for American astronauts and recognizes their historic 10-day mission. The crew not only traveled farther into space than anyone before but also helped prove the Orion spacecraft’s readiness for future deep space missions.

**One-sentence takeaway** – NASA’s Artemis II crew received top honors for safely completing the first crewed mission beyond the Moon in over five decades, setting a new record for human space travel.

articles.title: A ghostly ribbon of stars reveals hidden dark matter
articles.summary: A faint ribbon of stars around a distant galaxy has become the first globular cluster stellar stream ever identified beyond the Milky Way. Because the stars trace the galaxy’s gravity, researchers used the stream to estimate how much invisible dark matter surrounds it and how that matter is distributed. The breakthrough offers astronomers a promising new way to investigate one of the universe’s greatest mysteries.
articles.content:
For billions of years, an ancient cluster of stars has been gradually coming apart, shedding stars that now form a faint, narrow ribbon across space. That delicate structure is offering astronomers a new way to investigate one of the universe's biggest mysteries.

An international research team, including an astrophysicist from Northwestern University, has identified the first stellar stream of this type ever observed outside the Milky Way. Astronomers have long predicted that such streams should exist around other galaxies, but their extreme faintness has made them difficult to detect.

The newly discovered stream also offers scientists an unusual tool for studying dark matter, which remains one of the major unanswered questions in astrophysics. By analyzing the stream's shape, researchers reconstructed the gravitational field of its host galaxy and used that information to determine how unseen dark matter influenced the stars' paths.

The findings could eventually help scientists investigate how dark matter is distributed across many different galaxies and throughout the universe.

The study was published Aug. 12 in the journal Nature.

"The stars in a stellar stream all travel along nearly the same orbit, and that orbit is shaped by the galaxy's gravity," said Northwestern's Tjitske Starkenburg, who coauthored the study. "By modeling that gravity, we can estimate the galaxy's total mass. We already know roughly how much of that mass comes from visible matter like stars, so the rest must be dark matter."

Starkenburg, an expert in extragalactic astronomy, is a research assistant professor at Northwestern's Center for Interdisciplinary Exploration and Research in Astrophysics. The study was co-led by Julie Kiel Holm of the University of Copenhagen and Sarah Pearson of the Technical University of Denmark.

First Stellar Stream Found Beyond the Milky Way

Globular clusters are densely packed groups of stars held together by gravity. As one of these clusters travels around its host galaxy, the galaxy's gravitational pull can slowly strip stars away from it.

Those stars do not simply scatter in every direction. Instead, they tend to continue along nearly the same orbital path, creating long, thin stellar streams that retain information about the gravitational forces they have experienced.

Astronomers have identified dozens of streams produced by globular clusters inside the Milky Way. Until now, however, no comparable stream had been detected in another galaxy. Such structures are generally so faint that they disappear against the light of their host galaxies.

The breakthrough came through archival observations from NASA's Hubble Space Telescope presented by study coauthors David Sand and Catherine Fielder, both astronomers at the University of Arizona. While study coauthor David Hendel was examining images of the ultra-diffuse galaxy UGC 9050-Dw1 for their publication, he noticed a faint, narrow arc that looked like a stellar stream.

UGC 9050-Dw1 lies roughly 115 million light-years from Earth. Because the galaxy contains relatively few stars, it provided an unusually dark background that made the dim stream easier to distinguish.

A New Way to Measure Dark Matter

The importance of the discovery extends beyond finding the stream itself. Researchers have now shown for the first time that a globular cluster stellar stream can be used to investigate dark matter in a galaxy beyond the Milky Way.

Dark matter accounts for roughly 85% of all matter in the universe. Because it does not emit or reflect light, astronomers cannot see it directly. Instead, they detect its effects through the gravitational influence it exerts on stars, galaxies, and other visible objects.

Once the stream was identified, the team ran thousands of computer simulations. The researchers tested different combinations of globular cluster characteristics and possible dark matter distributions to determine which scenarios could reproduce the stream's observed appearance.

The models that most closely matched the observations provided new estimates of UGC 9050-Dw1's total mass and showed how that mass is distributed throughout the galaxy. The results indicated that UGC 9050-Dw1 contains a large amount of dark matter, as astronomers had expected for an ultra-diffuse galaxy.

"Our results are consistent with previous studies and what they have shown about dark matter in this ultra-diffuse galaxy," Kiel Holm said. "We are measuring it with a completely new tool for this type of galaxy, demonstrating that this method also works beyond our own galaxy."

Stellar Streams Could Expose Dark Matter Structure

Although the current analysis centers on just one galaxy, the finding could lead to searches for similar stellar streams around many different types of galaxies. With a larger sample, astronomers may be able to learn much more about how dark matter behaves and how it is distributed.

Thin stellar streams may be especially valuable because small concentrations of dark matter can potentially disturb them, producing visible gaps or clumps.

"Thin stellar streams can develop gaps or clumps when small concentrations of dark matter pass through them," Starkenburg said. "Astronomers have long debated whether we've seen this happen in streams within the Milky Way. If we can confirm that's what's causing these features, that will give us an entirely new way to test how dark matter is distributed -- and ultimately learn more about its fundamental nature."

New Telescopes Could Find Many More Streams

Future observatories could make these elusive structures much easier to find. The European Space Agency's Euclid mission and NASA's Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope are designed to survey far larger regions of the sky than Hubble, increasing the likelihood that astronomers will detect stellar streams around additional galaxies.

"It's exciting that we discovered a thin stellar stream around a galaxy other than our own with already-existing Hubble Space Telescope data and confirmed it with ground-based telescope data," Starkenburg said. "That makes it very promising for the new telescopes becoming available, including the Roman Space Telescope, which can see an area 100-times larger than that of the Hubble."

The study, "Evidence for the First Globular Cluster Stellar Stream beyond the Milky Way," was supported by VILLUM FONDEN (award number VIL53081) and the European Union (BeyondSTREAMS award number 101115754). Starkenburg also gratefully acknowledges support from the NSF (grant number AST-2510183) and NASA (grant numbers 22-ROMAN22-0055 and 22-ROMAN22-0013).

articles.personality_title: First stellar stream found beyond Milky Way helps map hidden dark matter
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – Stars often travel in groups called globular clusters. As these clusters orbit a galaxy, gravity can pull stars away, creating thin streams of stars. Until now, such streams had only been seen inside our Milky Way galaxy.

**What happened** – A team of scientists discovered the first globular cluster stellar stream outside the Milky Way. They found it around a distant galaxy named UGC 9050-Dw1, about 115 million light-years away, by studying images from NASA’s Hubble Space Telescope. The stream is a faint, narrow ribbon of stars that shows how the galaxy’s gravity affects them.

**Impact** – This discovery is important because the shape of the stellar stream helps scientists measure how much dark matter surrounds the galaxy. Dark matter is invisible and makes up most of the universe’s matter. By studying the stream, researchers estimated the galaxy’s total mass and confirmed that most of it is dark matter. This new method can help scientists understand dark matter in galaxies far beyond our own.

**What's next step** – Researchers hope to find more stellar streams around other galaxies using future space telescopes like NASA’s Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope and the European Space Agency’s Euclid mission. These telescopes will look at larger areas of the sky, making it easier to spot similar streams. Studying many streams could reveal how dark matter is spread across the universe and how it affects galaxies.

**One-sentence takeaway** – Scientists have found a stellar stream outside the Milky Way that offers a new way to study invisible dark matter in distant galaxies.
articles.personality_title_fr: Première détection d’un courant d’étoiles au-delà de la Voie lactée révèle la matière noire cachée
articles.personality_presentation_fr:
**Contexte** – Les étoiles voyagent souvent en groupes appelés amas globulaires. Lorsque ces amas tournent autour d’une galaxie, la gravité peut arracher des étoiles, formant ainsi des courants fins d’étoiles. Jusqu’à présent, ces courants n’avaient été observés que dans notre galaxie, la Voie lactée.

**Ce qui s’est passé** – Une équipe de scientifiques a découvert le premier courant d’étoiles d’amas globulaire en dehors de la Voie lactée. Ils l’ont trouvé autour d’une galaxie lointaine nommée UGC 9050-Dw1, située à environ 115 millions d’années-lumière, en étudiant des images du télescope spatial Hubble de la NASA. Ce courant est un ruban étroit et faible d’étoiles montrant comment la gravité de la galaxie les influence.

**Impact** – Cette découverte est importante car la forme du courant d’étoiles aide les scientifiques à mesurer la quantité de matière noire entourant la galaxie. La matière noire est invisible et constitue la majorité de la matière dans l’univers. En étudiant ce courant, les chercheurs ont estimé la masse totale de la galaxie et confirmé que la majeure partie est de la matière noire. Cette nouvelle méthode peut aider à mieux comprendre la matière noire dans des galaxies lointaines.

**Prochaine étape** – Les chercheurs espèrent trouver plus de courants d’étoiles autour d’autres galaxies grâce à de futurs télescopes spatiaux comme le télescope Nancy Grace Roman de la NASA et la mission Euclid de l’Agence spatiale européenne. Ces télescopes observeront de plus grandes zones du ciel, facilitant la détection de courants similaires. Étudier de nombreux courants pourrait révéler comment la matière noire est répartie dans l’univers et comment elle influence les galaxies.

**Phrase clé** – Des scientifiques ont découvert un courant d’étoiles en dehors de la Voie lactée qui offre une nouvelle méthode pour étudier la matière noire invisible dans des galaxies lointaines.
articles.personality_title_es: Primer corriente estelar fuera de la Vía Láctea ayuda a mapear la materia oscura oculta
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – Las estrellas a menudo viajan en grupos llamados cúmulos globulares. Cuando estos cúmulos orbitan una galaxia, la gravedad puede arrancar estrellas, creando corrientes delgadas de estrellas. Hasta ahora, estas corrientes solo se habían visto dentro de nuestra galaxia, la Vía Láctea.

**Qué pasó** – Un equipo de científicos descubrió la primera corriente estelar de un cúmulo globular fuera de la Vía Láctea. La encontraron alrededor de una galaxia distante llamada UGC 9050-Dw1, a unos 115 millones de años luz, estudiando imágenes del telescopio espacial Hubble de la NASA. La corriente es una cinta estrecha y tenue de estrellas que muestra cómo la gravedad de la galaxia las afecta.

**Impacto** – Este descubrimiento es importante porque la forma de la corriente estelar ayuda a los científicos a medir cuánta materia oscura rodea la galaxia. La materia oscura es invisible y representa la mayor parte de la materia en el universo. Al estudiar la corriente, los investigadores estimaron la masa total de la galaxia y confirmaron que la mayor parte es materia oscura. Este nuevo método puede ayudar a entender mejor la materia oscura en galaxias distantes.

**Próximo paso** – Los investigadores esperan encontrar más corrientes estelares en otras galaxias usando futuros telescopios espaciales como el Telescopio Nancy Grace Roman de la NASA y la misión Euclid de la Agencia Espacial Europea. Estos telescopios observarán áreas más grandes del cielo, facilitando encontrar corrientes similares. Estudiar muchas corrientes podría mostrar cómo se distribuye la materia oscura en el universo y cómo afecta a las galaxias.

**Frase clave** – Científicos han encontrado una corriente estelar fuera de la Vía Láctea que ofrece una nueva forma de estudiar la materia oscura invisible en galaxias lejanas.
